trial_name: HIGH WEAN — Effect of Postextubation High-Flow Nasal Cannula vs Noninvasive Ventilation on Reintubation and Postextubation Respiratory Failure in High-Risk Patients (2016)
citation: Hernández G, Vaquero C, Colinas L, Cuena R, González P, Canabal A, Sanchez S, Rodriguez ML, Villasclaras A, Fernández R. Effect of postextubation high-flow nasal cannula vs noninvasive ventilation on reintubation and postextubation respiratory failure in high-risk patients: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2016 Oct 18;316(15):1565-74.
one_liner: In high-risk ICU patients after planned extubation, HFNC was noninferior to prophylactic NIV for 72-hour reintubation and reduced postextubation respiratory failure with better tolerability.

pico.population: Adults mechanically ventilated >12 hours, planned extubation after successful SBT, with ≥1 high-risk feature for reintubation (age >65, APACHE II >12 at extubation, BMI >30, difficult/prolonged weaning, moderate-to-severe COPD, heart failure as indication for ventilation, >2 comorbidities, airway patency problems, inability to clear secretions, mechanical ventilation >7 days).
pico.intervention: HFNC started immediately after extubation; initial flow 10 L/min titrated up until discomfort; heated humidification at 37°C; FiO2 to SpO2>92%; applied for 24 hours, then conventional oxygen.
pico.comparison: NIV via full-face mask and BiPAP Vision ventilator, continuous for 24 hours; PEEP and pressure support adjusted to target RR 25/min and adequate gas exchange (SaO2≥92%, pH≥7.35); FiO2 to SpO2>92%; sedatives not allowed.
pico.outcome: Co-primary: all-cause reintubation within 72 hours and postextubation respiratory failure within 72 hours.

background.existing_knowledge: Postextubation respiratory failure and reintubation are frequent and associated with worse outcomes. Prophylactic NIV reduces reintubation in selected high-risk patients but is limited by intolerance and adverse effects.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether HFNC could replace NIV as postextubation prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients remained uncertain.
background.hypothesis: HFNC is noninferior to prophylactic NIV for preventing reintubation and postextubation respiratory failure within 72 hours in high-risk ICU patients after planned extubation.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, open-label, noninferiority trial; 3 ICUs in Spain; recruitment September 2012 to October 2014; registered (NCT01191489).
methods.setting: 3 ICUs in Spain; adult ICU; extubation after successful spontaneous breathing trial.

inclusion: Planned extubation after successful spontaneous breathing trial

≥1 predefined high-risk feature for reintubation: age >65 years; APACHE II >12 at extubation; BMI >30; difficult/prolonged weaning; moderate-to-severe COPD; heart failure as indication for ventilation; >2 comorbidities; airway patency problems; inability to clear secretions; mechanical ventilation >7 days

methods.intervention: HFNC started immediately after extubation; initial flow 10 L/min, increased by 5 L/min increments until discomfort. Heated humidification at 37°C; FiO2 titrated to maintain SpO2>92%. Applied for 24 hours, then switched to conventional oxygen.
methods.comparison: NIV started immediately after extubation via full-face mask and BiPAP Vision ventilator; planned continuous delivery for 24 hours. PEEP and inspiratory pressure support adjusted to target respiratory rate 25/min and adequate gas exchange (SaO2≥92%, pH ≥7.35); FiO2 titrated for SpO2>92%. Sedatives to improve tolerance were not allowed; after 24 hours, NIV was withdrawn and oxygen given by Venturi mask.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (clinicians and patients aware of treatment); outcomes included objective endpoints (reintubation, mortality) but also a composite “postextubation respiratory failure” construct with clinician-dependent elements.
methods.sample_size_power: 600 patients (300 per group) required to demonstrate noninferiority with an absolute margin of 10% (unilateral 95% CI; one-sided 5% alpha), assuming reintubation rate of 20%–25%, with 80% power and 15% allowance for attrition.
methods.primary_outcome: Co-primary: all-cause reintubation within 72 hours and postextubation respiratory failure within 72 hours.
secondary_outcomes: ICU and hospital length of stay
methods.follow_up: Co-primary outcomes to 72 hours postextubation; secondary outcomes to hospital discharge.

headline_bullets: HFNC met noninferiority for 72-hour reintubation (22.8% vs 19.1%; risk difference −3.7%; one-sided 95% CI −9.1 to ∞; margin 10%).
HFNC reduced postextubation respiratory failure (26.9% vs 39.8%; risk difference 12.9%; one-sided 95% CI 6.6 to ∞).
NIV was poorly tolerated: 42.9% required discontinuation vs 0% with HFNC.
ICU and hospital mortality were similar (ICU ~3%, hospital ~8%).

outcomes_table.note: Noninferiority margin 10% met; ITT and per-protocol consistent

outcomes_table.outcome: Postextubation respiratory failure due to hypoxaemia
Postextubation respiratory failure due to inability to clear secretions
ICU length of stay after randomisation (survivors), median (IQR)
outcomes_table.note: Total ICU LOS not significantly different

outcomes_table.outcome: Sensitivity analysis: reintubation excluding secretion-related criteria

safety: No HFNC discontinuations due to adverse events.
NIV discontinuation in 42.9% due to adverse events: discomfort 14.0%, facial skin erythema 6.4%, abdominal distension 4.1%.

domains.notes: Allocation concealed via independent telephone call centre. Simple randomisation (no blocking/stratification) led to unequal group sizes (314 NIV vs 290 HFNC), increasing susceptibility to chance imbalances.
ITT population 604/604; per-protocol 312/314 NIV and 288/290 HFNC (2 excluded per group); minimal attrition.

Open-label design; reintubation is objective but threshold-driven; postextubation respiratory failure criteria include clinician-dependent elements (secretion clearance, respiratory muscle fatigue), creating potential for differential classification.

Both strategies intended for 24 hours. NIV delivery attenuated: median duration 14 hours (IQR 8–23); 42.9% discontinued due to adverse events. HFNC delivered high flows: mean gas flow at 12 hours 50 (SD 5) L/min; FiO2 at 12 hours lower with HFNC (median 35% [IQR 30–40]) vs NIV (40% [35–50]). Prohibition of sedatives for NIV tolerance may have increased discontinuation and reduced effective separation of ventilatory support exposure.

High-risk profile achieved: median number of risk factors 3 (IQR 2–4) in both groups. Severity at extubation similar: APACHE II median 10 (8–12) NIV vs 11 (8–12) HFNC; PaO2/FiO2 during SBT 194 (148–261) vs 191 (149–251). Imbalances: heart failure as indication for ventilation 9.9% NIV vs 5.5% HFNC; surgical diagnosis 33.4% NIV vs 43.8% HFNC.

Both interventions started immediately postextubation, aligning with peak risk window. Rescue NIV after onset of postextubation respiratory failure was not allowed, limiting contamination but potentially influencing escalation thresholds.

Noninferiority assessed using one-sided 95% CI and prespecified absolute margin (10%). Primary outcomes reported in both ITT and per-protocol populations. Power adequate for co-primary noninferiority endpoints, not for mortality or small subgroup effects.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate to strong. Central randomisation, minimal attrition, and concordant ITT/per-protocol analyses support credibility; open-label delivery and substantial NIV discontinuation introduce meaningful risks of performance/detection bias and dose dilution for the active comparator.

domains.notes: Adult ICU cohort from 3 Spanish centres; all patients deemed “weanable” and extubated after successful SBT. Enriched for high-risk extubations; low-risk patients (466) excluded at screening, limiting inference to broader ICU extubation population. Hypercapnia during SBT was an exclusion (59 patients), limiting applicability to chronic hypercapnic respiratory disorders.

Requires HFNC infrastructure and staff familiarity; protocol used high flows (~50 L/min) with heated humidification. NIV protocol mandated continuous 24-hour application without sedative support; real-world NIV schedules and tolerance strategies vary. Findings most applicable to ICUs with similar extubation-readiness and reintubation thresholds; translation to step-down/ward environments uncertain.

external_validity.verdict: Good generalisability to non-hypercapnic, high-risk ICU extubations in centres with HFNC capability; limited generalisability to hypercapnic COPD populations or systems that deliver NIV with different dosing/tolerance practices.

strengths: Pragmatic multicentre randomised design with a clinically relevant high-risk population.
Co-primary outcomes focused on the early postextubation period (72 hours), when preventable failure is most likely.
Central allocation concealment; prespecified noninferiority margin; both ITT and per-protocol analyses for primary outcomes.
Very low loss to follow-up and clear reporting of adverse events and treatment discontinuation.
limitations: Open-label intervention and outcomes that include clinician-dependent components (especially the postextubation respiratory failure construct).
Simple randomisation caused unequal group sizes (314 vs 290) and some baseline imbalances.
Marked NIV intolerance and dose dilution (median 14 hours; 42.9% discontinuation), with sedatives prohibited.
Intervention duration fixed at 24 hours; optimal duration may differ by risk strata.
Exclusion of hypercapnia during spontaneous breathing trial limits inference for patient groups where NIV benefit may be greatest.

critical_appraisal.summary: HIGH WEAN is a well-conducted noninferiority trial demonstrating that HFNC is a viable alternative to prophylactic NIV in high-risk non-hypercapnic extubations, with better tolerability and similar reintubation rates, though open-label design and high NIV discontinuation may bias the comparison.
strengths: Pragmatic multicentre randomised design with a clinically relevant high-risk population.
Co-primary outcomes focused on the early postextubation period (72 hours), when preventable failure is most likely.
Central allocation concealment; prespecified noninferiority margin; both ITT and per-protocol analyses for primary outcomes.
Very low loss to follow-up and clear reporting of adverse events and treatment discontinuation.
weaknesses: Open-label intervention and outcomes that include clinician-dependent components (especially the postextubation respiratory failure construct).
Simple randomisation caused unequal group sizes (314 vs 290) and some baseline imbalances.
Marked NIV intolerance and dose dilution (median 14 hours; 42.9% discontinuation), with sedatives prohibited.
Intervention duration fixed at 24 hours; optimal duration may differ by risk strata.
Exclusion of hypercapnia during spontaneous breathing trial limits inference for patient groups where NIV benefit may be greatest.

sections.authors_conclusion: HFNC provided comparable (noninferior) protection against early reintubation to prophylactic NIV, while reducing postextubation respiratory failure and demonstrating markedly better tolerability. Hard outcomes (ICU and hospital mortality) were similar; the principal value proposition is reducing early respiratory deterioration and improving comfort, rather than mortality benefit. Supports a risk-stratified approach: HFNC as a default prophylactic support in many high-risk but non-hypercapnic patients, with NIV reserved for patients needing explicit ventilatory unloading (e.g., hypercapnic physiology or very high-risk phenotypes).

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: HFNC is noninferior to prophylactic NIV for preventing reintubation and reduces postextubation respiratory failure with better tolerability; it should be the default prophylactic strategy in high-risk non-hypercapnic extubations.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: High-risk ICU patients after planned extubation without hypercapnia during SBT, in centres with HFNC capability.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: HFNC does not replace NIV in patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure or those requiring explicit ventilatory unloading; it does not reduce mortality.
implementation_caveats: HFNC should be started immediately after extubation and continued for 24 hours.
NIV may still be considered for patients at very high risk or with hypercapnia, possibly in combination with HFNC.
Tolerance and adherence are critical; NIV discontinuation rates were high without sedation.

controversies.topic: Assay sensitivity in a noninferiority comparison
controversies.notes: Prophylactic NIV benefit is strongest in chronic hypercapnic respiratory disorders, while patients with hypercapnia during SBT were excluded; this complicates noninferiority interpretation if the active comparator effect is attenuated in the enrolled population.

Several elements used to classify “postextubation respiratory failure” (e.g., secretion clearance, reduced level of consciousness) have limited specificity for a respiratory cause and may be sensitive to clinician behaviour in an unblinded trial, potentially influencing both composite failure classification and reintubation decisions.

The investigators clarified that “inability to clear respiratory secretions” was intended as a criterion but was omitted from the printed definition of postextubation respiratory failure and later corrected; reanalysis excluding patients defined by secretion-related criteria reported reintubation in 73/314 (23.2%) NIV vs 48/290 (16.5%) HFNC (risk difference 6.7%; one-sided 95% CI 1.3 to ∞).

ERS/ATS clinical practice guidelines recommend prophylactic NIV after extubation in high-risk patients and recommend against routine NIV in low-risk patients; they also recommend against NIV as rescue therapy once postextubation respiratory failure is established. A large systematic review and network meta-analysis (36 RCTs; 6806 patients; searches through October 2021) found that, compared with conventional oxygen, both NIV (OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.52–0.82) and HFNC (OR 0.63; 95% CI 0.45–0.87) reduced reintubation, with no difference between NIV and HFNC (OR 1.04; 95% CI 0.78–1.38), and no short-term mortality benefit for either strategy. The HIGH-WEAN trial evaluated alternating NIV with HFNC vs HFNC alone after extubation in high-risk patients and reported lower reintubation with the combined strategy, supporting the concept that NIV may add benefit in higher-risk strata beyond HFNC monotherapy.

context_related_trials.relation: Recommend prophylactic NIV after extubation in high-risk patients; recommend against routine NIV in low-risk patients and against NIV as rescue therapy.
Found both NIV and HFNC reduce reintubation vs conventional oxygen, with no difference between NIV and HFNC, and no mortality benefit.
Reported lower reintubation with combined NIV+HFNC vs HFNC alone, supporting added benefit of NIV in higher-risk strata.

unresolved_questions: Optimal duration of postextubation prophylactic support.
Role of NIV in hypercapnic patients excluded from this trial.
Whether combined NIV+HFNC is superior to HFNC alone in the highest-risk subgroups.
Impact of sedation on NIV tolerance and efficacy.

numbers_to_remember: Reintubation: 22.8% HFNC vs 19.1% NIV (risk diff −3.7%, noninferior)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In high-risk non-hypercapnic extubations, HFNC is noninferior to NIV for reintubation and reduces postextubation respiratory failure with far better tolerance, making it the preferred first-line prophylactic strategy.
